concepts.name: Battery
concepts.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

concepts.name: Control of the centre
concepts.wording: Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.

Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.

concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concepts.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concepts.name: The principle of two weaknesses
concepts.wording: A single weak point is holdable because every defender can gather around it. Fix it so it cannot be repaired, improve your own pieces while the opponent has nothing to do, then open a second front on the far wing. The defence cracks in transit between the two, not at either one.
cautions: Targets too close together: if the defending king can shuttle between both, the mechanism largely fails. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending - moving the kings from g1/g8 to d3/d6 drops the evaluation from +1.74 to +0.75.

Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.

concept.name: Passed pawn
concept.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. cautions: MEASURED 2026-09-02: a knight against a bishop is not an imbalance by this record's own preferred numbers - Kaufman puts a knight and an UNPAIRED bishop at the same 3.5 - and the matcher fired on every such swap, 42.1% of the 788 shipped positions. It is a third name for a fact `bishop-pair` and `bad-bishop` already report. concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concepts.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

cautions: Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.

concepts.name: Rook on the seventh rank
concepts.wording: A rook on the seventh rank: it attacks pawns from a side they cannot defend and confines the king. It is decisive mainly when the king is trapped on the eighth behind it — if the king is out, the rook is good rather than winning.
cautions: A rook reaching the seventh is not decisive by itself. With an empty seventh rank and an enemy king that has luft, a tested position evaluates level at -0.04.
The king escaping forward removes most of the value at a stroke.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Centralisation of the king
concepts.wording: Centralisation of the king: once queens are off and mating attacks are unlikely, the king becomes an active piece and often the strongest one. It attacks weak pawns, escorts passed pawns and blockades enemy ones, and the side whose king arrives first usually wins endings that look level.
cautions: Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.

concepts.name: Doubled pawns
concepts.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.
